stories.title: Sex, spies and salaries shake up AI chipmakers
stories.summary: Hello everyone, this is Cissy from Hong Kong.
stories.title_zh: Sex, spies and salaries震动AI chipmaker行业
stories.content:
Hello everyone, this is Cissy from Hong Kong.

Unless you've been offline since the weekend, your social media feeds have probably been swamped, like mine, with posts about the affair between Nvidia's chief Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, or Huang Le in Chinese. They range from reports by major media outlets to AI-generated memes and videos poking fun at the topic of the moment, likely powered by Nvidia chips.

An acquaintance who briefly overlapped with Huang at CCTV confirmed to me that she spent a short stint at the state broadcaster as an "intern reporter" about 20 years ago, before leaving for the more lucrative financial sector.

On social media, a carnival of unverified group photos said to be from her middle school graduation, screenshots of her WeChat posts showing off her close relationship with Jensen, and even her old business card as a partner at Shanghai private equity firm Hexi Investment have circulated.

Meanwhile, the buzz centers on whether Ms. Huang is a Chinese spy, an allegation The New York Times reported, citing senior U.S. policymakers. The allegation has sparked heated debate over whether the label fits at all, since the definition of a "spy" can be stretched very broadly.

Multiple U.S. media outlets reported Thursday morning that besides Alice, Jensen had a romantic relationship with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, and its board has been holding an urgent meeting, amid speculation he will be ousted.

## **Asian workers aim to close the AI pay gap**

While the multi-billionaire's leadership fate hangs in the balance, it is already clear that the semiconductor boom that propelled Nvidia to the top and made his fortune has also created a vast wealth divide across Asia - a gap that shows little sign of narrowing anytime soon.

While the U.S. has historically offered higher wages than other countries for talent, workers in Asia, especially in South Korea and Taiwan, are beginning to push back against stagnant compensation, demanding a larger share of the profits of the AI boom, Nikkei Asia's **Kim Jaewon, Steven Borowiec**, **Cheng Ting-Fang, Lauly Li,** and **Cissy Zhou** reported this week.

After an all-out strike, Samsung Electronics management agreed to pay 10.5% of its memory unit's operating profit as a special bonus to department employees, worth up to 700 million won ($520,000) for a regular worker. Meanwhile, workers at SK Hynix are snapping up properties in Seoul suburbs with their generous bonuses, with average monthly home purchases near the company's headquarters doubling in the first half compared to a year earlier.

The AI pay-gap discontent has also spread to Taiwan. A union dispute at U.S. memory chipmaker Micron's subsidiary on the island has led to salaries for mid- to senior-level engineers nearly tripling and a major bonus-payment deal that will apply to workers globally.

## **Alice Huang's checkered China past**

Alice Huang is no stranger to scandal, write the FT's **Eleanor Olcott** and **Zijing Wu**.

For years, she worked with Kang Wei, a financier who was both a romantic partner and business associate, even as he faced multiple investigations for stock market violations in China.

The FT reported this week that the pair pitched China-based investors in early 2025, touting their ability to secure highly prized Nvidia GPUs and their close business ties to Chinese tech group Alibaba.

The relationship between Alice Huang and Kang also illustrates the checkered network of connections surrounding the Chinese businesswoman and raises further questions about the Nvidia chief's decision to entwine his business and his personal life with hers.

## **Japan's Sakana AI readies major IPO**

Japanese artificial intelligence developer Sakana AI is preparing for an initial public offering either in Japan or the U.S. as early as autumn 2027, Nikkei's **Rei Nakafuji** and **Akira Yamashita** have learned.

The IPO could give it a market valuation above the 680 billion yen ($4.3 billion) that Japan's first unicorn Mercari achieved in 2018.

Sakana was established in 2023 and achieved unicorn status just a year later. It is developing a homegrown AI model, tentatively named "Sakana Sawara." It plans to release a small-scale model in the spring of 2027 before developing a larger one.

A year ago, it reached a 400 billion yen valuation in a private placement of shares with investors including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, the highest valuation ever achieved by an unlisted Japanese startup. Nvidia and Google are also investors.

## **Grab, SoftBank invest in Malaysia AI infrastructure**

Grab and SoftBank Group will invest $1.85 billion in AI infrastructure projects, including data centers, in Malaysia, betting on surging digital demand across Southeast Asia. The planned projects will provide at least 5 gigawatts of AI computing capacity, Nikkei Asia's **Kentaro Takeda** writes.

Under the plan, two projects - one in Peninsular Malaysia and the other in the eastern state of Sarawak - will be built.

The first $850 million will go toward the Peninsular Malaysia project, with Grab footing $650 million of the bill and SoftBank putting up the remaining $200 million. For the Sarawak project, SoftBank will contribute $800 million, while Grab and local energy group Petroleum Sarawak Berhad (Petros) will each invest $100 million.

stories.title: Huawei Digital Power launches four innovative solutions to power next-generation data centers
stories.summary: New power, energy storage, and liquid-cooling innovations target greater efficiency, reliability, and sustainability in AI infrastructure
stories.title_zh: 华为数字能源发布四项创新解决方案，为下一代数据中心供能
stories.content:
Huawei Digital Power unveiled four innovative data center infrastructure solutions at the Huawei Digital Power Data Center Innovation Summit & New Product Launch 2026, held at Sofitel Dubai The Palm under the theme *“Power the AI Era Forward.”*

The newly introduced portfolio includes the UPS5000-H modular uninterruptible power supply (UPS), PowerPOD 5.0 integrated power solution, SmartLi 5.0 lithium-ion battery system, and Liquid-Cooling Thermal Management Unit (TMU). Together, these solutions are designed to address the growing demands for power reliability, energy efficiency, deployment speed, and intelligent operations in next-generation AI data centers.

As AI accelerates the growth of computing infrastructure, data center operators face increasing challenges in managing higher power densities, complex cooling requirements, and continuous availability.

To address these challenges, Huawei Digital Power integrates bit, watt, heat, and battery (4T) technologies, bringing together expertise in high-density computing power supply, liquid cooling, energy storage, and intelligent power management to deliver more efficient, resilient, and sustainable data center infrastructure.

### UPS5000-H: High reliability, efficiency, and density

The UPS5000-H modular uninterruptible power supply delivers up to 99.9999 percent reliability, 99.1% efficiency in S-ECO mode, and 800 kVA capacity per cabinet. Its modular design enables highly reliable power protection while reducing energy losses and optimizing space utilization in mission-critical data centers.

### PowerPOD 5.0: High-density integrated power solution

PowerPOD 5.0 delivers 3.2 MW of power capacity in a 40-foot configuration, reducing the power system footprint by 40% and shortening deployment time from seven to three days. With a 0.5-percentage-point efficiency improvement and AI-enabled predictive maintenance, the solution supports faster, more efficient data center deployment and operations.

### SmartLi 5.0: Intelligent and safe energy storage

SmartLi 5.0 is a next-generation lithium-ion battery solution designed for high reliability and advanced safety in data centers. Compatible with emerging 800V HVDC architectures, it incorporates multi-level fault isolation and positive-pressure oxygen-blocking technology to enhance battery safety and support resilient power infrastructure.

### Liquid-Cooling TMU: Intelligent cooling for AI computing

Huawei's Liquid-Cooling TMU portfolio offers cooling capacities ranging from 450 kW to 1,380 kW, supporting diverse high-density AI computing environments. Featuring AI-powered leakage detection as low as 0.02 L/min and coolant health prediction up to seven days in advance, the solution enhances cooling reliability and enables proactive maintenance.

## Powering the next generation of AI data centers

The launch of these four solutions reflects Huawei Digital Power's broader strategy to accelerate innovation across the entire data center infrastructure ecosystem. By combining its capabilities in renewable power generation, grid-forming technologies, high-density power supply, liquid cooling, and computing-power synergy, Huawei aims to address the evolving energy and infrastructure requirements of AI-driven computing.

As the industry enters a new era of accelerated AI adoption, Huawei Digital Power is committed to becoming a leading innovator in intelligent computing data center infrastructure and a long-term, trusted strategic partner for customers worldwide. Through close collaboration with global customers and ecosystem partners, the company aims to advance high-quality, sustainable innovation, enabling greener watts, more tokens per watt, and lower costs per token.

With its latest portfolio, Huawei Digital Power continues to support the transition toward highly reliable, energy-efficient, and intelligently managed data centers, helping operators build the foundation for the next generation of AI computing.

KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 13): Malaysia’s benchmark stocks may end Friday at a fresh 14-month low as investors continued to trim investments related to data centres.

The 30-stock FBM KLCI dropped as much as 4.6 points or 0.3% to 1,581.35, its lowest since September 2025. National electric utility firm Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) fell 1.6% to RM12.60 while construction firm Gamuda Bhd (KL:GAMUDA) was down over 2% to RM4.58.

After five consecutive sessions of decline, the benchmark index is also set to end Friday with over 2% weekly loss. Correction in artificial intelligence trades and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia’s leadership could trigger further selling pressure in the near term.

Analysts, however, see opportunities for bargain hunting.

“We believe the market has entered oversold territory, potentially setting the stage for a technical rebound in the coming weeks,” Malacca Securities Sdn Bhd head of research Loui Low Ley Yee told *The Edge*.

December is historically a good month for the FBM KLCI, with a success rate of over 90% over the past 25 years, suggesting a potential upside of 2% to 3% towards year-end, he said.

Jensen Huang has stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia following news reports of his extramarital affairs while shares of the US chip giant continued to fall.

Nvidia is also reeling from revelation over the weekend about Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy accused of helping entities circumvent American restrictions on imports of high-performance chips to China.

stories.content:
(Nov 13): Southeast Asia risks facing tighter US regulations on the export and use of high-powered chips, threatening to stall the region’s AI-fuelled economic boom.

The fallout from Nvidia Corp chief Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy working at a firm with ties to Singapore and Malaysia has increased scrutiny of the shipment and use of US-restricted chips in Southeast Asia.

Some in the Trump administration fear that places such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand have been weak points in global efforts to keep the most advanced tech from China — either as transit points for the diversion of the chips or as hosts to data centres with restricted chips that are used remotely by Chinese firms.

While Huang’s exit removes one of the most high-profile proponents against stringent restrictions in Washington, the scale of the expected tightening is still unclear.

Legislation that may pass by the end of the year could include firmer restrictions on the sale of high-end chips to foreign countries. As well, the US Commerce Department is looking at imposing new export rules and licensing requirements to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore, according to the *Wall Street Journal*.

Governments are already seeking to assuage the security concerns. Singapore charged a fifth person on Friday in relation to an AI server fraud case, while Malaysia is investigating whether AI chips brought into the country have been subsequently shipped overseas.

“This would put a dampener on the demand for AI compute in existing and future data centres in Southeast Asia,” said Malaysia’s former deputy trade minister Ong Kian Ming, adding that new laws further restricting access and use would be hard to mitigate and manage for governments in the region.

“Malaysia would take the brunt of the likely drop in demand but this may also have spillover effects to Thailand and Indonesia,” he said. “Singapore also may not be spared if this limits the ability of some of the AI players” registered in the city-state.

Data centres have emerged as an unexpected growth driver for Southeast Asia this year, alongside the boost from semiconductor and related AI exports, offsetting the drag from higher oil prices and interest rates.

Chinese demand for computing capacity in Southeast Asia could be reduced, introducing greater risk to the data centre investment pipeline, according to Brian Lee, an analyst for Maybank Securities Pte Ltd.

Malaysia and Thailand have been hotspots for data centre investments, while Indonesia’s data centre market is in earlier stages of development, Lee said.

“Data centre investment demand is nonetheless also driven by domestic cloud demand, digital services and the broader digital economy, which may not require the advanced Blackwell class Nvidia GPUs under proposed export controls,” he added.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul was likewise sanguine, saying Friday that US and Chinese firms alike have reaffirmed their commitment to invest in the country. Senior Indonesian minister Airlangga Hartarto said his country has been in talks with Washington about a US-led effort to secure global AI and semiconductor supply chains.

Southeast Asia’s appeal is hinged on its attractive power, land and regulatory environment for hyperscalers, according to a September report by Goldman Sachs Group Inc.

“Another driver is export-control arbitrage, as Chinese players can use Asean as a platform for deploying US chips in model training for non-China markets,” it said.

It’s unclear exactly how much of Southeast Asia’s computing resources have been tapped by Chinese firms, as buyers of Nvidia chips have been reluctant to disclose the identities of their clients. But within the industry the demand is seen as a major driver of the region’s data centre boom.

Goldman forecasts Southeast Asia’s data centre capacity would grow fourfold in the next five years, with the Malaysian state of Johor to be the largest hub in Asean by 2030. It estimates Malaysia should see an average growth boost of 30 basis points from 2026 to 2028, while Thailand gets an additional 20 basis points.

Cameron Systermans, who heads Asia multi-asset for consultancy Marsh, said the region may see “more selectivity, rather than a broad retreat” in light of the Nvidia fallout.

The fundamental drivers of the region’s data centre build out remain strong, as AI adoption and cloud use expand rapidly, he said. Southeast Asia is a strategic location for investors seeking to diversify supply chains and build digital capacity closer to fast-growing markets.

“The most attractive markets and projects will be those that can combine growth potential with reliable infrastructure, transparent investment structures, and a stable regulatory environment,” he said. “Capital will become more discerning.”

stories.summary_zh: 日本两大银行集团SMFG和Mizuho报告了更强的年度利润，但警告AI data center投资势头可能放缓，这是主要金融机构对digital infrastructure罕见的看空信号。

stories.content:
TOKYO (Nov 13): Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group and Mizuho Financial Group on Friday raised their profit forecasts for the financial year but flagged the prospect of a slowdown in investment into AI data centres.

SMFG boosted its annual earnings forecast to ¥1.9 trillion from ¥1.7 trillion and expanded its share buyback programme as corporate lending demand from local firms remained strong and higher domestic interest rates increased lending margins.

Net profit over the July to September quarter was ¥501.8 billion (US$3.14 billion or RM12.8 billion), down 10% from a year earlier, when it registered a gain of ¥94 billion on the sale of its stake in India's Kotak Mahindra Bank.

Mizuho also raised its annual profit forecast to ¥1.6 trillion from ¥1.4 trillion and doubled the size of its share buyback programme this financial year to ¥400 billion. The company generated ¥473.6 billion in net profit over the July to September period, 19% higher than the year before.

A slowdown in data centre investment could hit the Japanese and global economies and impact SMFG's results over the next six months, chief executive officer Toru Nakashima said at a press briefing.

"This year we have adopted stricter standards on extending credit for data centre financing, for instance restricting ourselves to just hyperscalers with high credit standing," Nakashima said.

Mizuho CEO Masahiro Kihara flagged greater restrictions on data centre construction in the US as a tail risk as the results of the midterm elections last week brought sweeping wins for the Democratic Party, which could slow projects and so bring about higher development costs.

Fears of overheating in global data centre investment and rising political opposition have led to a sharp decline in technology stocks in recent weeks as investors reassess their exposure to the vast sums flowing into AI infrastructure.

The resignation of the chief executive of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs has sparked concern over the chipmaker's continued ability to spearhead data centre projects as it both supplies chips and finances the infrastructure built around them.

"The impact of Huang stepping down is difficult to see at present and whether it leads to a slowdown in data centre investment will depend on the new management," SMFG's Nakashima said.

"Personally, I don't think their stance will change that significantly," he added.

SMFG increased its share buyback programme by ¥220 billion, bringing the total shares to be bought up to ¥400 billion for the financial year that ends in March 2027.

KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 13): There has been no indication that artificial intelligence chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue were exported from Malaysia, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.

“There has not been any indication of that (so far),” he told reporters on Friday when asked whether there was evidence that the chips had been exported from the country.

Anwar also said the Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) had given a report on the matter on Friday morning.

“We will cooperate with all the agencies involved,” he said when met after he had performed Friday prayers at Madrasathul Gouthiyyah at Brickfields.

To a question on whether Malaysia had received a formal request from Singapore or the United States regarding any probe on the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue, Anwar said Malaysia has not received any formal request from Singapore or the United States regarding the issue.

“Right now, we have not received any such request. But we will, of course, collaborate.

“Ours is a trading nation. We welcome investments. We want to make sure the rules are being followed,” he said.

In a statement earlier on Friday, Miti said it had never cleared Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte Ltd or its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd.

Miti said Speedmatrix is a tenant at data centres in Malaysia and brings its own servers and AI chips into the country for its operations.

The ministry said it was working with the Royal Malaysian Customs Department to determine whether any of those chips had been re-exported to other countries and, if so, whether the re-exports complied with Malaysian laws.

Miti said no permit or licence is currently required to bring AI chips into Malaysia.

However, since July 2025, anyone seeking to export, re-export, transship or transit high-performance US AI chips from or through Malaysia must first obtain a permit from Miti under the Strategic Trade Act 2010, the ministry said.

It said giving false information to Customs about such goods is also a serious offence under the Customs Act 1967.

Miti said Malaysia would carry out its own checks independently, in accordance with Malaysian laws based on the available evidence.

stories.title: Australia data centre capacity to nearly double by 2030
stories.summary: Australia's data center market is projected to expand by 2.3GW through 2030, effectively doubling national capacity, though Melbourne is capturing more development momentum as Sydney faces delays tied to power availability and planning approvals.
stories.why_it_matters: The geographic shift from Sydney to Melbourne redistributes investment and jobs within Australia while highlighting how energy constraints are becoming the primary bottleneck for data center growth in developed markets, potentially reshaping where hyperscalers and colocation providers commit capital.
stories.title_zh: 澳大利亚数据中心容量到2030年将接近翻倍
stories.summary_zh: 澳大利亚data center市场预计到2030年将增加2.3GW，基本实现全国容量翻倍，尽管由于电力供应和规划审批问题导致悉尼项目延迟，墨尔本正获得更多开发动力。
stories.why_zh: 从悉尼到墨尔本的地理转移重新分配了澳大利亚国内的投资和就业，同时凸显出能源限制正成为发达市场data center增长的主要瓶颈，可能重塑hyperscale和colocation提供商的资本投向。
stories.content:
Fri, 13th Nov 2026 (Today)
Data Centres Australia has published a new forecast on the Australian data centre market, pointing to continued growth in capacity and a wider spread of development beyond Sydney and Melbourne.

Produced with market intelligence firm DC Byte, the report tracks 163 operational data centres across Australia and puts current operational capacity at 1.6GW. It forecasts capacity will rise to 3.9GW by 2030, up from an earlier projection of 3.2GW, alongside 97 additional facilities.

The figures also show a sharp rise in projects moving through the development pipeline. Total forecast pipeline capacity has increased by 5.2GW since the previous edition, while capacity under construction has doubled over the same period.

That growth in construction is evenly split between Sydney and Melbourne, but the pattern at earlier development stages has shifted. Melbourne has seen more capacity move from early stage to committed status than Sydney, at 1.2GW compared with 0.7GW.

By contrast, Sydney's total pipeline and early stage capacity have both declined, with total pipeline capacity down 3.6GW and early stage capacity down 4.4GW. The report links the fall to energy constraints, policy approval timelines and recent policy changes.

Melbourne's total pipeline has increased by 1.7GW and now exceeds Sydney's. Early stage projects in Melbourne rose by only 0.3GW, suggesting much of the change came from projects advancing to later stages rather than from a surge in new proposals.

### Market shifts

The report also points to a geographic shift in where data centre projects are being planned. Over two years, the share of the total pipeline outside Sydney and Melbourne has risen from 19% to 31%.

These projects include early stage developments in Queensland, Tasmania, South Australia and Western Australia. The report says energy constraints, policy settings and government investment signals are shaping where operators and customers choose to locate projects.

DC Byte's approach differs from tallies based mainly on announced schemes or connection applications. The report's methodology assesses project viability and aims to distinguish between projects more likely to proceed and speculative schemes that may never reach the market.

That distinction matters in a sector where demand projections can generate large headline numbers that do not always translate into built capacity. Its segmented approach is intended to support evidence-based policy and planning by focusing on what is more likely to be delivered.

Demand for cloud services and AI compute is identified as a central driver of the expected rise in capacity. At the same time, planning processes, energy availability and policy differences between states are emerging as stronger influences on where development occurs.

Belinda Dennett, Chief Executive Officer, Data Centres Australia, said the report was intended to provide a more measured view of the market. "Australia is a highly attractive market for sustainable data centre development, with a leading industry ecosystem and attributes such as large-scale renewable energy generation. Credibly tracking data centre growth requires nuance and our report is designed to help cut through the noise by qualifying project viability," Dennett said.

She said project activity had continued to strengthen since the previous report. "Capacity under construction has doubled since our April report and more capacity has moved from early stage to committed, demonstrating continued demand in the market," Dennett said.

### State contrast

The clearest contrast in the latest figures is between Victoria and New South Wales. The report says Victoria's gains may reflect faster approval processes under the state government's Development Facilitation Program, while projects in New South Wales face the State Significant Development process and a less certain approval timetable.

Dennett pointed to the recent shift in Victoria's numbers. "The analysis shows pronounced growth in the data centre pipeline in Victoria over the last six months, likely attributable to the state government's efforts to attract investment. We expect recent changes in policy may have an impact on whether this continues," Dennett said.

She said the spread of projects beyond the two main east coast hubs was likely to continue as new forms of demand reshape siting decisions. "The numbers also reveal a trend for development outside the major hubs of Sydney and Melbourne. We expect to see this pattern continue as new workloads like AI and neoclouds increase demand and bring different siting requirements. We are also seeing current energy constraints and different policy approaches influence customer and operator decisions," Dennett said.

stories.title: Samsung is in talks to acquire data centre cooling firm Modine
stories.summary: The potential deal will help the firm diversify, as it is too reliant on its memory business, notes analyst

stories.title_zh: Samsung洽谈收购数据中心冷却公司Modine
stories.content:
The potential deal will help the firm diversify, as it is too reliant on its memory business, notes analyst

\[NEW YORK\] Samsung Electronics is in talks to acquire Modine Manufacturing, a maker of cooling systems for data centres, according to people familiar with the matter.

The companies are discussing a potential transaction that could come together as soon as the coming weeks, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

No final decision has been made and the talks could still fall apart, the people said. Another suitor could also emerge, they added.

Representatives for Samsung and Modine declined to comment.

Modine’s shares closed regular trading on Thursday (Nov 12) in New York at US$106.10, giving the company a market value of about US$5.6 billion. The stock soared to more than US$135 in late trading, a gain of 28 per cent.

The company’s shares had fallen about 15 per cent since Nov 3, when it reported quarterly results that underwhelmed investors.

Samsung rose as much as 3.9 per cent in Seoul on Friday, before paring gains. The stock has surged 72 per cent in 2026 so far, giving the company a market value of about US$910 billion.

“An acquisition of Modine would help Samsung diversify into other areas, given the group is too dependent on its memory business,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Masahiro Wakasugi said.

“While it can generate a lot of cash from chips, it might need to find other growth businesses such as data centre-related assets.”

The discussions underscore how mergers and acquisitions is picking up around companies that cater to the booming artificial intelligence market.

US companies and their overseas rivals have stepped up efforts to capture the growth opportunity coming from data centres through bigger investments and dealmaking.

Among them are Samsung’s Asian rivals Daikin Industries and LG Electronics, as well as US-based Vertiv.

Based in Racine, Wisconsin, Modine makes heavy duty cooling and heating systems for large commercial buildings and industrial machines, with its fastest-growing business serving hyperscalers that build data centres.

In October, the company spun off its automotive business to focus on its thermal-management operations.

“Modine recently became a pure-play thermal management business and has huge upside to data centre cooling solutions, with the unit growing 86 per cent annually for the past three fiscal years,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Christina Feehery said.

“Still, it’s seen as a small peer relative to the larger HVAC OEM market, making it an attractive target for vertical integration in AI infrastructure.”

Samsung is one of the largest technology and electronics companies in the world. The Suwon, South Korea-based company’s products include smartphones, televisions, home appliances, thermal solutions and computer memory chips.

While a Modine takeover would be bolder in magnitude, Samsung has been bolstering its thermal solutions offering to data centres through international acquisitions. It purchased Germany-based FläktGroup for 1.5 billion euros (US$1.7 billion) in 2025. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Malaysia denies clearing Megaspeed, checks for illegal chip re-exports
stories.summary: Firm’s Malaysian affiliate Speedmatrix imports its own servers and AI chips for use at rented data centres in country, says Miti
stories.title_zh: 马来西亚否认批准Megaspeed，检查非法芯片再出口
stories.content:
Firm’s Malaysian affiliate Speedmatrix imports its own servers and AI chips for use at rented data centres in country, says Miti

\[JOHOR BAHRU AND KUALA LUMPUR\] Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) has clarified that it has never cleared Singapore-based Megaspeed International or its Malaysian affiliate Speedmatrix, and is actively reviewing whether artificial intelligence chips brought into the country have been improperly re-exported.

In a statement on Friday (Nov 13), Miti said Speedmatrix, a tenant at Malaysian data centres, brings its own servers and AI chips into the country for its operations.

Importing AI chips does not currently require a permit or licence. However, exporting, re-exporting, transhipping or transiting high-performance US AI chips from or through Malaysia has required a Miti permit under the Strategic Trade Act 2010 since July 2025.

Providing false information to customs about such goods is also a serious offence under the Customs Act 1967, it added.

The ministry also highlighted that the routine verification visits to data centres occupied by Speedmatrix were part of its regular monitoring of the sector and should not be interpreted as clearing the companies of wrongdoing.

“Any verification visits carried out by Miti at these facilities are part of its regular monitoring of the data centre sector, and should not be taken to mean that a company has been cleared. Any suggestion otherwise is inaccurate,” it said.

The clarification comes amid scrutiny of Megaspeed over suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. Bloomberg has reported that the US Justice Department was working with the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security on the investigation.

Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani had earlier said the ministry had not been presented with evidence that Speedmatrix had breached Malaysian law.

## Checks across jurisdictions

Miti is working with the Royal Malaysian Customs Department to determine whether chips brought into Malaysia were subsequently re-exported and whether those shipments complied with the law. Its statement did not announce any finding of wrongdoing.

Malaysia would conduct its checks independently under domestic law and based on available evidence, the ministry said. It was also working closely with authorities in Singapore and the US, and considering further measures to strengthen controls.

Separately, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday that investigations into Megaspeed and six individuals remained ongoing.

Singapore authorities were examining whether servers exported through the city-state to Malaysia had subsequently been routed elsewhere, contrary to declarations made in Singapore.

Megaspeed said on Thursday that it had cooperated with US inspections and retained a US law firm to conduct a comprehensive inventory of its graphics processing units (GPUs) and independently verify its export-control compliance practices.

Miti said that while Malaysia does not enforce other countries’ unilateral export controls, companies operating locally were expected to take those restrictions into account in their international business.

It also warned companies against misrepresenting their dealings with government agencies.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centres and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” the ministry said, adding that stern action would be taken against companies found to have broken Malaysian law.

## Quiet Johor office

A directory at Eco Galleria, a commercial development in Iskandar Puteri in Malaysia’s southern state of Johor, listed Speedmatrix at three units when BT visited on Friday.

Records from the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM), the country’s corporate registry, list one of those units as MSFusion’s registered address.

Malaysian-listed Crescendo Corp previously identified MSFusion, the buyer of a RM263.2 million parcel of land for a data centre, as a Megaspeed subsidiary. BT saw no signage bearing MSFusion’s name at the premises, nor was it included in the directory at Eco Galleria.

Speedmatrix’s office interior was obscured from view, and no activity was apparent during the visit. A worker at a neighbouring business said she had seen staff entering and leaving on other days.

## Regional footprint

According to *The Straits Times*, Megaspeed operated seven overseas subsidiaries in 2024, including three in Malaysia: cloud providers Speedmatrix and Megaspeed International, alongside MSFusion – a dormant firm that later acquired RM263.2 million (US$64.5 million) of Johor land for a data centre in August 2025.

Megaspeed also owned majority or full stakes in entities across Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, and the US.

Additionally, corporate intelligence platform Sayari records show an Nvidia GPU baseboard shipment arrived for Speedmatrix on Nov 18, 2025.

stories.title: Asian tech stocks rebound after Nvidia upheaval
stories.summary: Upheaval at Nvidia is testing the AI trade without derailing the broader investment boom
stories.title_zh: Nvidia动荡后亚洲科技股反弹
stories.content:
Upheaval at Nvidia is testing the AI trade without derailing the broader investment boom

ASIAN stocks edged higher as investors eased back into technology shares amid fading concerns that a leadership crisis at Nvidia may derail the broader artificial-intelligence trade.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index rose 0.4 per cent, led by a gain of over 2 per cent for South Korean shares. US equity futures also advanced, with Nasdaq 100 contracts up 0.4 per cent and those for the S&P 500 gaining 0.3 per cent after both underlying benchmarks fell on Thursday (Nov 12).

Nvidia, the company at the heart of the AI boom, dropped as much as 14 per cent after chief executive officer Jensen Huang was ousted, but dip buyers stepped in, leaving it just 4.3 per cent lower by the close.

US oil broadly held its gains, trading around US$88.50 a barrel after President Donald Trump said the US could forgo a deal with Iran.

US Treasury yields mostly held near Thursday’s highs as traders braced for faster Federal Reserve rate hikes, while a gauge of US dollar strength was little changed. Gold steadied after a three-session decline and Bitcoin traded around US$71,100.

The upheaval at Nvidia is testing the AI trade without derailing the broader investment boom. Instead, it may make investors more selective, favouring companies best placed to benefit from continued spending.

“This is going to be a more differentiated story and players that have stronger balance sheets that are more focused on doing the hard work of that community engagement are likely to be the winners in this next stage of the build-out,” Mike Pyle, deputy head of BlackRock’s Portfolio Management Group, said in an interview on Bloomberg Television.

That shift was already evident on Wall Street. Shares of Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices, which compete with Nvidia in parts of the AI chip market, rallied over 5 per cent as investors sought potential beneficiaries from the industry leader’s setback.

Nvidia’s market capitalisation briefly dropped below US$4 trillion with revelations about Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, rattling investors ahead of earnings.

A related probe into suspected spy Alice Huang and efforts to smuggle Super Micro Computer products to China sent that company’s shares down as much as 16 per cent, the most in more than five months.

“Nvidia’s earnings already demand close attention, but they will be under an even brighter spotlight next week,” said Bret Kenwell at eToro. “Investors will be looking to Nvidia for a fresh read on demand and a reason to regain confidence.”

Two other events next week may provide a broader test of appetite for the AI trade: Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO and CoreWeave’s plan to raise at least US$4 billion through an investment-grade loan offering. Strong institutional demand for Anthropic suggests appetite for AI exposure remains robust.

In Asia, traders will also be watching the yen after it weakened past 160 per US dollar for the first time since September, reviving the prospect that Japanese authorities may intervene to support the currency.

“Markets are jittery about potential FX intervention whenever we approach the 160 area,” said Win Thin, chief economist at Bank of Nassau 1982.

Higher oil prices added to pressure on Treasuries, extending a sell-off sparked on Tuesday by hotter-than-expected inflation and signals that Fed officials may favour more aggressive rate hikes. Policy-sensitive two-year yields edged lower after climbing 14 basis points on Thursday.

On Thursday, Fed New York president John Williams said that US inflation remains high and that policymakers have to take further action to contain price pressures.

“Investors continue to pencil in more rate hikes,” said Gennadiy Goldberg, head of US interest rates strategy at TD Securities. While setbacks for US technology shares – which benefited Treasuries last month – “could short-circuit the bearish move at some point, the macro underpinnings are the ones driving Treasuries right now.” BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Data centers adopt new power procurement strategies
stories.summary: Data center operators are exploring new strategies for power procurement, moving beyond traditional grid connections. This shift is driven by increasing power demand and challenges with public grid supply.
stories.title_zh: 数据中心采用新电力采购策略
stories.content:
Data centers are consuming more power than ever, prompting many operators to adopt new strategies for securing energy. The era of simply connecting to the public grid may be ending as operators pursue creative solutions.One approach involves power purchase agreements (PPAs), which are contracts allowing data centers to buy electricity at a fixed price from a utility or power producer. PPAs can improve price predictability and support faster access to new power capacity.PPAs also enable data centers to financially support the expansion of clean energy generation, reducing reliance on fossil fuels without building their own renewable plants.
### On-site Generation and Microgrids

Behind-the-meter power involves installing on-site generators to meet most or all of a facility’s energy needs. This expensive strategy offers greater control over energy sources and helps avoid grid interconnection delays.Microgrids represent another emerging strategy, relying on a network of on-site or nearby generators and small-scale power resources. Microgrids typically imply a more distributed system with multiple energy sources, enhancing resilience and potentially including energy storage infrastructure.
### Phased Energization and Grid Contribution

Phased energization addresses situations where the public grid cannot supply a data center’s full power requirements immediately. Facilities begin operations incrementally as power becomes available, allowing partial deployment sooner rather than waiting years for full grid capacity.Some hyperscalers are also experimenting with front-of-the-meter power, using on-site generation to supply electricity back to the broader grid. This strategy may help address concerns about data centers straining the grid and contributing to rising electricity costs.

- Energy, Cooling & Sustainability

stories.title: Data Center World brings new opportunities for Nidec
stories.summary: Nidec, a major supplier of motors and cooling systems, is leveraging its first appearance at Data Center World in Singapore to initiate partnership discussions with operators and cloud providers seeking AI-optimized thermal management solutions.
stories.why_it_matters: Nidec's market entry underscores how AI workload density is redrawing the competitive landscape for data center cooling, where traditional HVAC incumbents face challenge from specialized suppliers; successful partnerships could accelerate adoption of liquid cooling and high-efficiency motors across Southeast Asian facilities struggling with tropical heat and power constraints.
stories.title_zh: Data Center World为Nidec带来新机遇
stories.summary_zh: 电机和冷却系统主要供应商Nidec正利用其在新加坡Data Center World的首次亮相，与寻求AI优化thermal management解决方案的运营商和云提供商启动partnership discussions。
stories.why_zh: Nidec的市场进入凸显了AI工作负载密度如何重塑data center cooling的竞争格局，传统HVAC老牌企业面临专业供应商的挑战；成功的partnerships可能加速东南亚 struggling with tropical heat and power constraints 的设施采用liquid cooling和high-efficiency motors。
stories.content:
Nidec Corporation is expanding its push into the data center market, targeting operators and cloud service providers as demand for thermal management solutions grows alongside artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The Japanese manufacturer reported strong interest in its data center cooling technologies at Data Center World Asia in Singapore, where it exhibited for the first time, securing potential customer leads and opening discussions with prospective strategic partners.

Nobuyasu Nozawa, deputy head of AI & IT Division SPMS at Nidec Corporation, said the exhibition had generated significant inquiries from data center operators and cloud service providers, as well as opportunities to collaborate with manufacturers of complementary cooling equipment.

The company is positioning its thermal management expertise as a key differentiator as it seeks to establish itself as a significant supplier to the data center industry.

### Pursuing new customers

Data Center World Asia represented Nidec's second appearance at a Data Center World exhibition, following its earlier appearance at Data Centrer World in Washington, DC.

While the Singapore exhibition attracted international interest, Nozawa said the most significant outcome was the quality of commercial discussions held with potential customers and partners.

The company received inquiries from data center operators and cloud service providers, including organisations interested in its in-row coolant distribution unit (CDU) technology from all around Asia including its home country, Japan.

CDUs are used in liquid cooling systems to manage the circulation and distribution of coolant, helping remove heat from computing equipment. As AI workloads increase the thermal demands placed on servers, liquid cooling is becoming an increasingly important component of data center infrastructure.

Nozawa said several prospective customers had visited Nidec's booth to discuss specific business opportunities.

"We received a lot of visitors at Data Center World," Nozawa said.

"A lot of attention was paid to our latest products and solutions. It was a really good show for Nidec."

For Nidec, the event provided an opportunity to engage with the broader ecosystem surrounding AI infrastructure, rather than limiting its outreach to traditional equipment customers.

### Cooling partnerships offer route to market

Beyond direct customer inquiries, Nidec identified potential partnerships with manufacturers of other cooling equipment as an important outcome of its exhibition in Singapore.

Nozawa said several chiller manufacturers approached the company throughout the event to discuss combining their products with Nidec's in-row CDUs.

The proposed arrangements would allow the companies to offer complementary cooling technologies to data center customers as part of a more integrated solution.

Chillers and CDUs perform different functions within cooling infrastructure. Chillers help remove heat from a facility's cooling system, while CDUs manage coolant distribution closer to the IT equipment.

Combining the technologies can help suppliers address different parts of a data center's thermal management requirements.

The discussions extended beyond Southeast Asia, with companies travelling from Japan and India to meet Nidec representatives in Singapore.

The company has since begun follow-up conversations with prospective partners, including chiller manufacturers in Japan.

Nozawa described the discussions as a significant outcome of the exhibition, pointing to tangible opportunities for collaboration, as the company looks to expand its partner base in Japan, as well as other markets.

Instead of relying exclusively on direct sales, the company is looking to become part of a wider network of manufacturers delivering integrated cooling solutions.

### Thermal expertise underpins expansion

Nidec is seeking to use its established thermal management capabilities to build credibility with data center customers.

Nozawa said the company's history in cooling technologies, spanning air cooling and more recent work in liquid cooling, distinguished it from competitors entering the market.

Nidec's experience across different generations of thermal solutions provides the foundation for its ambitions in data center infrastructure.

The company's strategy reflects the growing importance of heat management as data centers accommodate increasingly demanding computing workloads.

AI infrastructure can place substantial thermal loads on servers, increasing the need for efficient cooling systems capable of maintaining operating conditions while supporting higher computing density.

For equipment manufacturers, this creates opportunities to supply technologies that address cooling requirements at both the server and facility levels.

Nidec is aiming to position itself as a thermal specialist supplier in this market, using its existing engineering and manufacturing capabilities to support the needs of data center operators and their equipment partners.

The interest generated at Data Center World Asia shows that Nidec is beginning to build those connections.

### Asian manufacturing base supports customers

Nidec is also highlighting its established presence in Asia as an advantage in pursuing data center opportunities across the region.

Nozawa said the company's Japanese heritage and design operations in Japan and manufacturing operations in Asia allow Nidec to support customers throughout the region.

Having key capabilities and manufacturing resources close to customers can be valuable during the deployment of specialised cooling infrastructure, particularly when projects require inspections.

"From our design center in Japan and the manufacturing location in Thailand, we can support the customers in this area particularly closely. For the initial inspection or installation, or what we call commissioning, or a factory visit by the customer, it's very easy, actually."

For Nidec, the focus is now on converting the interest generated at Data Center World Asia into commercial opportunities and strategic partnerships.

The Singapore exhibition marked an early step in its effort to establish a stronger presence in the data center supply chain, with liquid cooling and collaboration with complementary equipment manufacturers emerging as central elements of its approach.

stories.title_zh: Nvidia CEO离职加剧行业抛售，全球AI股票下跌
stories.content:
Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and some chip stocks fall

\[BENGALURU/SYDNEY\] Global artificial intelligence-linked stocks fell on Thursday (Nov 12) after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a deepening scandal around his affairs, upending the chipmaker’s leadership and posing fresh risks to a sector already reeling with funding and regulatory concerns.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the company said.

As the centrepiece of the AI ecosystem, the chipmaker finances infrastructure built around its chips – a strategy that has drawn scrutiny over circular funding and now risks weighing on the sector as its crisis deepens.

AI stocks have struggled after the Democrats swept the midterm elections, including in states opposed to new data centres, stoking fears that tighter regulation could slow the AI infrastructure build-out.

Nvidia’s shares fell 8.2 per cent to a more than 16-month low in early trading and its market value was on track to close below US$4 trillion for the first time since July 2025.

Nvidia-backed neocloud firm CoreWeave dropped 9.1 per cent after surging more than 27 per cent in the previous session when its earnings ignited a relief rally in AI stocks.

Other neocloud stocks including IREN and Applied Digital were also trading lower. Nebius dropped 16.2 per cent after the company said its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its previous forecast.

Nvidia has lost more than US$550 billion in market value since the board announced an investigation on Sunday into Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.

“He’s the face of Nvidia and Nvidia has been front and centre of the AI build-out,” said Jun Bei Liu, lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.

“And if we look at how many new cloud data centre businesses have been sponsored in this circular financing world, it’s pretty much all by Nvidia. And so it has quite a meaningful ramification for what is to come.”

Nvidia short sellers have made US$9.6 billion in on paper profits so far this week, according to data analytics firm Ortex.

Chipmakers, widely viewed as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, led the sell-off, with the Philadelphia chips index sliding 1.3 per cent.

Marvell Technology, which Huang called the “next trillion dollar company” in June, slumped 3.8 per cent. AI hyperscaler Oracle, which is expanding its cloud AI chip deals with Nvidia, shed 2.6 per cent.

Memory chipmaker Micron Technology fell 2.5 per cent; data storage firms Sandisk and Western Digital eased 6 and 3.7 per cent, respectively. Photonic product makers Lumentum and Coherent and AI server maker Dell eased between 3 and 5.1 per cent.

Construction and power-generation equipment maker Caterpillar and power producer Vistra slipped about 0.5 per cent each.

Shares of AMD and Broadcom, which also produce AI chips and compete with Nvidia, however, rose 3.7 and 5.6 per cent, respectively, on expectations that the turmoil at Nvidia could create opportunity for rivals.

Other hyperscalers including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft were also up between 0.8 and 2.7 per cent.

AI stocks struggled and the Nasdaq entered a technical correction earlier this month after the Democrats swept the midterm elections, including in states opposed to data centres, stoking fears tighter regulation could slow the AI build-out.

Tech-heavy stock markets across the globe witnessed jitters. Japan and South Korea closed nearly 0.7 per cent lower. Tech stocks in Europe were also down about 1 per cent.

Nvidia trades at about 12 times its 12-month forward earnings estimates, its lowest since November 2012, according to data compiled by LSEG. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: US to restrict Chinese remote access to AI chips from Southeast Asian data centers: Report
stories.summary: The US reportedly plans to bar data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, Norway, and South Africa from letting Chinese AI companies remotely access advanced AI chips, expanding export control enforcement beyond physical shipments to cloud-based compute access.
stories.why_it_matters: This fundamentally changes how Chinese AI firms can access compute globally, forcing them to rely on domestic or fully controlled infrastructure rather than Southeast Asian colocation and hyperscale facilities that had become popular workaround destinations. Data center operators in the targeted countries may see demand soften from Chinese customers while competing for non-restricted workloads.
stories.title_zh: 美国将限制中国企业从Southeast Asian data centers远程访问AI芯片：报告
stories.summary_zh: 据报道，美国计划禁止马来西亚、新加坡、泰国、印度尼西亚、巴西、挪威和南非的data center允许中国AI公司远程访问其advanced AI chips，将出口管制执法范围从实体发货扩大到云端算力访问。
stories.why_zh: 这从根本上改变了中国AI公司获取全球算力的方式，迫使其依赖国内或完全受控的基础设施，而非已成为热门变通目的地的东南亚colocation和hyperscale设施。受影响国家的data center运营商来自中国客户的需求可能减弱，同时需要争夺不受限制的工作负载。
stories.content:
Data centers in Southeast Asia including Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia are among seven countries that will soon be restricted by the US from allowing Chinese AI firms to remotely access their advanced AI chips, The Information reports today quoting people familiar with the process.

The other three countries are Brazil, Norway and South Africa. The proposed US Commerce Department rules would require licences for exports of Nvidia Blackwell-class and more advanced chips to these destinations. The aim is to prevent Chinese AI firms from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through data centers in other countries as well as preventing chip smuggling into China.

The rule could be announced as soon as this month. It will expand existing semiconductor-related controls from the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security. The department is currently consulting with other government agencies on the long-awaited rule before finalizing it.

In recent days, the US government has been criticized for being too slow in implementing policies to restrict China’s access to advanced AI technologies. In the wake of Nvidia’s recent alleged spying scandal, the criticisms have grown louder. Nvidia has long opposed any restrictions on chip sales to China.

stories.title: CDC files to develop 1.4GW data center campus in Kemps Creek, Australia
stories.summary: CDC has submitted planning documents to develop a 1.4GW data center campus at Kemps Creek in Western Sydney, representing one of the largest single data center projects proposed in Australia.
stories.why_it_matters: The sheer scale of 1.4GW tests whether Australia's grid and planning systems can accommodate hyperscale concentration in a single location, and its approval or rejection will set precedents for how other massive projects navigate energy availability and community opposition in the country.
stories.title_zh: CDC提交在澳大利亚Kemps Creek开发1.4GW数据中心园区的申请
stories.summary_zh: CDC已提交规划文件，计划在澳大利亚西悉尼Kemps Creek开发一个1.4GW的data center campus，这是澳大利亚拟议的最大的单一data center项目之一。
stories.why_zh: 1.4GW的庞大规模将检验澳大利亚电网和规划系统能否在单一地点容纳hyperscale集中部署，其获批或被拒将为其他大型项目如何在该国应对能源供应和社区反对树立先例。
stories.content:
CDC this month filed an updated SEARS application with the New South Wales government for a new campus at Kemps Creek.

The company originally filed an application in August to develop a single four-story building, totaling 144MW across 34,000 sqm (365,970 sq ft), on 88.4 hectares at 871-901 Mamre Road.

CDC has now filed an updated application, increasing the scope of the project. The company is now looking to develop six two-story buildings (KC1 to KC6) totaling 1.4GW, as well as an on-site substation, across 117.5 hectares at 859-901 Mamre Road.

The original application was set to be the first stage of a wider campus to be expanded over additional filings, with the new application representing the entire campus under a single filing.

The first three buildings are set to offer 168MW across five data halls; building four will offer 144MW across four halls; building five 120MW across three data halls; and building six 240MW across seven halls.

Founded in 2007 and backed by investment firm Infratil, CDC has nearly 20 sites in operation and development across Sydney, Canberra, Melbourne, and Auckland, New Zealand.

It has more than 600MW of data center capacity in operation and development across Melbourne, Sydney, Canberra, and New Zealand (70MW). The company’s future development pipeline now totals a further 1.6GW out to 2034.

Sydney is currently home to two CDC campuses, Eastern Creek and Marsden Park.

Eastern Creek has four buildings live – EC1 offers 7MW, EC2 20MW, EC3 42MW, and EC4 54MW. Work started on the site in 2018, and two more are under construction (EC5 and EC6) that could total more than 100MW.

Still in development, Marsden Park could offer more than 504MW of capacity with potential to scale to around 1GW. The company broke ground on the site in late 2024.

stories.title: MUFG enters MoU with Japanese industry coalition to build satellite mega-constellation
stories.summary: Feasibility study between Japanese champions explores integrated multi-role sovereign constellation
stories.title_zh: 三菱日联金融集团与日本产业联盟签署谅解备忘录，建设卫星巨型星座
stories.content:
A coalition of Japanese tech firms and financial companies has joined together for a planned satellite constellation.

Japanese bank holding and financial services giant Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Inc. (MUFG) has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, NTT, Inc., NTT Docomo Business Inc., and the Development Bank of Japan Inc. to examine the technical and business feasibility of developing a satellite mega constellation, serving communications, Earth observation, disaster response, positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), national security, and orbital data centers (ODCs) serving customers in Japan and overseas.

This remit effectively spans and extends beyond the functionality of the European Copernicus, Galileo, and IRIS² constellations.

“The five companies will combine their respective technologies, customer bases, financial capabilities, and business development expertise to pursue the realization of a … mega-constellation business,” the companies’ statement reads.

The proposition is more than ambitious, suggesting the kind of advanced and integrated capability that Starlink, Starshield, and “Starmind” are beginning to build out today, despite the three initiatives resembling the most mature integrated constellation in the world.

The project champions the interpretation that satellites are social infrastructure, going on to suggest space data centers can empower more efficient utilization of satellite data to “address a wide range of social issues.”

“MUFG Bank regards the space industry as a vital component of social infrastructure with the potential to address a wide range of societal challenges,” said Yuichiro Moto, managing executive officer and group head of MUF’s Corporate Banking Group, in the statement. “Drawing on our experience in leveraging satellite data, our expertise as a financial institution, and our extensive customer base across a wide range of industries in Japan and overseas, we will contribute to developing the space industry’s value chain and addressing diverse societal challenges.”

The constituent companies, each speculated on their contribution to the coalition in their combined statement:

- Consumer electronics manufacturer Mitsubishi Electric, the only company in the coalition that has made a satellite before, would conduct technical studies on the system design and integration of the constellation.
- Japan’s telecommunications giant, NTT, would explore the feasibility of a comms network between space and ground, commercialization, and R&D from its AI-centric information and communications infrastructure (IOWN) project.
- NTT’s international arm, NTT Docomo Business, would explore use cases and customer needs.
- MUFG itself would support the development of businesses, supply chains, and sales channels.
- Sovereign wealth entity, the Development Bank of Japan, would explore long-term commercialization and opportunities for intersectionality across industry, government, academia, and the financial sector.

In June, Mitsubishi Electric acquired the satellite ground station-as-a-service (GSaaS) company Infostellar for an undisclosed sum, empowering the company’s ground segment resources.

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI), which launches the H3 medium-lift space rocket and is the most prominent company with Mitsubishi in its name that does space technology – visible at space conferences worldwide – is absent from the would-be zaibatsu.

Considering the apparent sovereign focus, MHI would be the supposed mega-constellation’s route to orbit, meaning its constituent satellites will need to be compatible with H3 or its successor.

stories.title: Malaysia raises by 10 times penalty for data center phantom power demand: Report
stories.summary: Malaysia has increased its connected load charge for data centers nearly eleven-fold to RM89.64 per kilowatt, a punitive rate designed to stop operators from reserving grid capacity they do not actually use.
stories.why_it_matters: The dramatic fee hike forces data center developers to align contracted power with actual deployment timelines, penalizing speculative land-banking and phantom demand that had been congesting Malaysia's grid; this should improve allocation efficiency but may slow pre-sales and project announcements in the near term.
stories.title_zh: 马来西亚将data center phantom power demand罚款提高10倍：报告
stories.summary_zh: 马来西亚将data center的connected load charge（CLC）提高了近11倍至每千瓦RM89.64，这一惩罚性费率旨在阻止运营商预留实际不使用的电网容量。
stories.why_zh: 这一大幅费用上涨迫使data center开发商将合同电力与实际部署时间线对齐，惩罚一直在挤占马来西亚电网的投机性土地囤积和phantom demand；这将提高配置效率，但可能短期内减缓预售和项目公告。
stories.content:
Malaysia has hiked the connected load charge (CLC) from RM8.50 to RM89.64 per kilowatt, a dramatic 10.55 times or 955 per cent higher to deter phantom or speculative power demand by data centers, local reports said yesterday quoting Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.

Phantom demand is power capacity reserved by developers which is then unutilised causing stranded capacity and unused infrastructure. CLC is a penalty for demand falling below the reserved demand capacity. It is calculated monthly on the shortfall between actual maximum demand (actual usage) and reference maximum demand (reserved demand).

“Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) would have already planned its infrastructure and allocated capacity to accommodate full declarations, leaving unused megawatt capacity that could otherwise support other users,” Johari reportedly said at an event in Kuala Lumpur.

Last month, Parliament was informed about the hike, however, the revised rate and effective date were not mentioned.

TNB, Malaysia’s electricity utility still shows the old rate on its website at press time. w.media reached out to TNB to confirm the new rate and its date of implementation but has yet to receive a reply to date.

Malaysia has also established a new ultra high voltage tariff category which requires developers or operators to fully bear the cost of transmission upgrades.

Data center investment in Malaysia has seen exponential growth surging from 0.4 per cent of total approved investments of RM1.25bil in 2021 to 43.9 per cent or RM95.8 billion in 1H 2026. The country, which is enroute to becoming the biggest data center hub in Asia (ex China) has approved 117 data centers which has a combined maximum energy demand of about 23,500 megawatts (MW).

Out of 117 approved data centers, 55 are operational, 19 are under construction, 16 are approved but yet to start, and 27 have been approved for off-grid energy supply. About 24 applications are still waiting for approval.

stories.title_zh: Nvidia动荡加剧，YTL Power恢复下跌，data centre pick-and-shovel trade受挫
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 12): Shares related to data centre investments in Malaysia fell on Thursday, led by YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR), amid reports of renewed turmoil at Nvidia.

YTL Power alone lost over RM3 billion in market capitalisation as shares of the multi-utilities firm resumed their decline, dropping 39 sen or over 8% to RM4.40. Nearly 41 million shares changed hands, making YTL Power one of the most actively traded stocks on Bursa Malaysia.

The company, now valued at RM38 billion, is a data centre partner of Nvidia and operates a facility powering artificial intelligence in Johor equipped with some of the US chipmaker's latest chips.

The declines follow news reports of another extramarital affair of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, this time with a company executive who reported to him. The *Wall Street Journal* reported that Nvidia was preparing to oust Huang as the American chip giant’s stock continued to fall.

The latest reports come even as Nvidia was reeling from revelation over the weekend about Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy accused of helping entities circumvent American restrictions on imports of high-performance chips to China.

YTL Corp Bhd (KL:YTL) extended its losses and declined 11 sen or 5.56% to settle at RM1.87, valuing the parent company of YTL Power at RM22.06 billion.

NationGate Holdings Bhd (KL:NATGATE), a contract manufacturer for Nvidia, retreated 12 sen or 6.42% to RM1.75.

Real estate firms developing data centres, such as Mah Sing Group Bhd (KL:MAHSING), Sime Darby Property Bhd (KL:SIMEPROP), Gamuda Bhd (KL:GAMUDA), Sunway Construction Group Bhd (KL:SUNCON) and IJM Corp Bhd (KL:IJM) were also caught in the selldown.

Mah Sing's share price dropped six sen or 6.63% to settle at 84.5 sen, Sime Darby Property slid one sen or 0.78% to RM1.27.

Gamuda's share price sank 22 sen or 4.49% to RM4.68, Sunway Construction Group declined by 28 sen or 3.35% to RM8.07 and IJM Corp Bhd (KL:IJM)'s shares price fell 10 sen or 3.83% to RM2.51.

stories.title_zh: Goldman称AI将在2027年继续主导美国企业投资
stories.content:
(Nov 12): Goldman Sachs on Wednesday forecast annualised spending on artificial intelligence-related hardware and intellectual property will climb to US$1.4 trillion (RM5.7 trillion) by the end of 2027, equivalent to nearly 4% of the US economy.

"AI will remain the dominant driver of business investment growth in 2027," the brokerage said, forecasting spending to exceed US$900 billion by the end of 2026.

The view comes amid concerns that rising borrowing costs and increased investor scrutiny could curb AI-related capital spending, particularly as companies lean more heavily on debt-funded expansion.

Democrats' victories in the US midterm elections earlier this month sparked concerns over tighter regulation of data-centre development, but Goldman Sachs said the outcome poses only limited risks to AI investment.

Goldman estimates AI-related investment will directly boost 2027 capex growth, including semiconductor investment by 5.3 percentage points and US GDP growth by 0.6 percentage points.

"Semiconductor investment is undercounted in the business investment statistics, and most information processing equipment is imported and is thus netted out of GDP," Goldman said.

Excluding semiconductor investment, AI-driven investment will boost 2027 capex growth by 4.3 pp and US GDP growth by only 0.2 pp, the brokerage said.

Overall, Goldman forecasts US business investment growth at 8% on a quarterly basis in 2027, nearly double the consensus forecast of 4.2%.

stories.title: Nvidia fallout puts trade truce to the test as Xi welcomes Trump
stories.summary: Espionage allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's interactions have complicated the trade relationship between the US and China just as Chinese President Xi Jinping prepares to welcome President Trump, potentially undermining recent diplomatic progress.
stories.why_it_matters: The timing transforms a corporate governance issue into a geopolitical flashpoint, putting Nvidia at the center of US-China negotiations and potentially making the chipmaker's operations a bargaining chip that could reshape market access rules for the entire semiconductor and data center supply chain.
stories.title_zh: NVIDIA余波考验贸易休战，习近平迎接特朗普
stories.summary_zh: 围绕Jensen Huang互动的间谍指控使中美关系复杂化，正值中国国家主席习近平准备迎接特朗普总统之际，可能破坏近期的外交进展。
stories.why_zh: 这一时机将公司治理问题转化为地缘政治导火索，使Nvidia处于中美谈判的中心，并可能使该芯片制造商的运营成为筹码，从而重塑整个半导体和data center供应链的市场准入规则。
stories.content:
Spy allegations engulfing the chipmaker’s CEO Jensen Huang reopen old rifts

XI JINPING’S third summit of 2026 with US President Donald Trump is going off script before their meetings even get underway, as the spy allegations engulfing Nvidia’s Jensen Huang reopen old rifts.

For years, Huang had been most the prominent US tech executive advocating for greater engagement with China as he lobbied for looser export controls on semiconductors.

Now, bombshell accusations he conducted an affair with an alleged Chinese spy are giving lawmakers in Washington ammunition to tighten curbs, days before a major leaders’ summit in the Chinese technology hub of Shenzhen.

At stake is a year-long trade truce between the world’s top economies expiring in January – its renewal hinges, in large part, on the US pausing new restrictions on tech shipments to China.

David Perdue, America’s top diplomat in Beijing, on Wednesday (Nov 11) signalled the furor was posing a test to bilateral relations during an already “bumpy” stretch.

The scandal is only deepening. Fresh reports that Huang had multiple extramarital affairs have cast further doubt over his future, with Nvidia’s board now working to identify a potential replacement chief executive officer, according to a person familiar with the matter.

For some in Beijing, the timing of the revelations has drawn attention.

Reports of Huang’s affair only exploded into full view in the aftermath of the Republicans’ midterms wipe-out that weakened Trump – a longtime backer of Nvidia’s CEO, who is one of the world’s most powerful figures in US artificial intelligence.

Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of the *Global Times*, claimed leaks by US intelligence services were “driven by calculated political motives”.

“China is suffering collateral damage from internal strife in the US,” said Wang Yiwei, a former Chinese diplomat and director of Renmin University’s Institute of International Affairs.

“The Democrats achieved such a dramatic turnaround in the midterms not only because of pushback to Trump – it also reflects public backlash against the alliance between Silicon Valley’s tech giants and financial capital.”

So far, there is no sign the Nvidia saga will derail the truce.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent – who manages the US economic relationship with China – hailed progress in ties this week at an event with the Chinese ambassador to Washington Xie Feng.

Any fallout would have ramifications for the global economy. Some US$500 billion in annual trade in goods and services between the US and China is at stake as they approach a deadline for renewing their truce.

When Xi hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering next week, investors will be closely watching for any signals from Trump on export controls and – if Huang survives – whether he brings along the Nvidia chief, whom the US leader endorsed this week as an “honourable guy”.

In May, Huang jumped on Air Force One at the last minute at a refuelling stop in Anchorage, joining Trump’s trip to Beijing at the personal invitation of the president.

Some American lawmakers and foreign policy analysts are already calling on the White House to respond by imposing more export controls to diminish advanced semiconductor flows.

One option would be widening curbs to capture subsidiaries majority-owned by already-sanctioned firms – the so-called 50 per cent rule that has been suspended until January is regarded by some in Washington as the key to closing a major loophole.

“This is the first major test of the truce,” said Jeff Moon, president of China Moon Strategies and former Assistant US Trade Representative for China Affairs.

“If it’s true that Chinese espionage tried to, or did steal, Nvidia technology, then the US has to respond,” he said.

“At the core of the truce were US commitments not to increase tech restrictions, and Chinese agreement to provide critical minerals. So this episode gets right at the heart of the tech restrictions.”

The face-off is bringing to the surface tensions that were already brewing between the US and China.

Earlier in November, Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer raised concerns with China’s Vice-Premier He Lifeng about the importance of implementing commitments made as part of the trade deal reached by Trump and Xi in South Korea a year ago.

Central to that is the flow of rare earths used to make everything from mobile phones to missiles.

While the US secured supplies of such critical minerals under the truce, officials including Greer have repeatedly said that America is not getting the metals at the expected volume and pace. From the US to Japan, manufacturers are feeling the squeeze.

That non-compliance, combined with recriminations following the Nvidia scandal, may give new momentum to efforts by some in the US to put relations under more scrutiny.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has come out in support of provisions in 2026’s National Defense Authorization Act that would restrict China’s access to chips.

Congress is also currently advancing the Chip Security Act. That would force technology companies to physically track advanced processors through the supply chain, making it significantly harder for restricted AI chips to reach China via unauthorised intermediaries.

“For Beijing, the risk is that an investigation into individual conduct becomes a justification for broader technology restrictions on Chinese companies,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

That could make ordinary business contact “more politically sensitive”.

With Huang now diminished, finding common ground will be harder still.

The timing of the scandal may reflect that “some people in the intelligence community are not happy with Trump’s approach to China,” said Wu Xinbo, director at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies in Shanghai.

Ultimately, more curbs would only deepen Beijing’s push for self-reliance, he added: “Further controls will certainly help companies like Huawei who would like to keep the Chinese market closed to US products.” BLOOMBERG

stories.why_zh: 这种 preemptive capacity抢购正在加速东南亚和其他中介市场对colocation和hyperscale空间的需求，但如果美国限制措施落地，这些锁定的capacity中大部分可能无法供中国客户使用，为接受这些预订的data center运营商带来合同纠纷和财务风险。
stories.content:
Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies are attempting to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres located outside China, according to three people familiar with the matter.This action stems from concerns that a controversy involving Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, could prompt Washington to tighten restrictions on remote access to advanced processors.US export controls currently limit the direct export of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China. However, Chinese firms can bypass these restrictions by renting computing power from overseas data centres that utilise such processors.A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally securing overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some companies have contacted data centre operators for reservations. Smaller AI labs are also exploring similar steps, including approaching major providers in Southeast Asia, two of the people said.These companies reportedly fear that the controversy surrounding Huang could add political momentum to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). This proposed US bill would grant the Commerce Department authority to regulate cloud-based access to restricted technology. The House of Representatives passed RASA in January, and it awaits Senate action.Advanced Nvidia processors are crucial for training and running large AI models that power chatbots and other generative AI products. Restricting overseas cloud access would make it more difficult for Chinese developers to obtain high-end computing power without direct chip imports.
### Market and Enforcement Concerns

The prospect of tougher enforcement has also increased demand for restricted Nvidia AI chips in China's grey market. Traders and intermediaries have begun stockpiling these processors, two of the sources stated. Buyers fear the controversy could lead to a broader US crackdown on smuggling advanced chips and AI servers into China.Procurement records indicate that a Chinese university, despite being on a US export blacklist, purchased Nvidia H200 AI chips last month. This highlights existing gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology.US prosecutors in March charged Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and two others with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips to China. This was allegedly done through a Southeast Asia-based company that bought approximately $2.5 billion of servers from Super Micro between 2024 and 2025.

stories.summary_zh: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang据称与一名现涉及间谍指控的中国商人会面，暴露了该公司命运与其创始人个人行为和关系的紧密关联。
